If two groups draw the edge differently, compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave its floor plan unmarked. Yesterday’s patch belongs in yesterday’s drawing. # Watching the Light

A drawing is a choice about what to notice. In this booklet we will notice one thing: where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor.

## What we will do

The activity takes place over three school days. You will work with the same partner each day. You will make an observation at the beginning of the morning lesson and another immediately after lunch. That gives six observations in all.

We do this more than once because one drawing cannot show whether a position changes. It shows only where the light was, once. Several drawings can show more.

Our drawings will show where the light can be seen. They will not tell us why it is there. That is a different question, and the drawings do not answer it.

## How to mark the floor plan

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan. Write the time beside it.

Sometimes the edge of the light is fuzzy. Where it is, draw that part with a dotted line. Do not decide that the edge must be sharp just because a sharp line is easier to draw. A pencil and ruler are provided, but the ruler does not make a fuzzy edge less fuzzy. It is good for straight lines. It cannot tell you where the light ends.

You may find that another group has marked the edge differently. Do not change your drawing straight away, and do not tell them to change theirs. First compare what each of you noticed. Then decide whether either drawing needs to change.

## When there is no light

Some days the patch may not be visible. When that happens, write "no patch visible" in the space for that observation. Leave the map unmarked. Do not draw where the patch was yesterday. That would be a map of yesterday.

"No patch visible" counts as an observation. It does not count as a measurement of the patch's position, because there was no position to measure.

The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds, and we will not record how thick they are. So we will not know why a patch is missing. We will know only that we did not see it.

## At the end

Compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Then write:

- one sentence about a pattern you can support
- one question that remains

Perhaps too few patches were visible to show a pattern. If so, say that, and explain which observations are missing.

You are not required to discover a particular pattern. A careful account of what could not be observed can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in the desktop application’s **Reading settings**. Turn it on to pause the application’s spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control. By default, descriptions continue speaking when focus moves, just as they did before.

When Pause on Focus is enabled, returning focus to the image does not automatically resume the description. Use the existing **Read Description** command to hear it again from the beginning. “Pause” means that speech stops while the saved description is kept; it does not mean you can resume from the word where it stopped. The setting does not change the descriptions themselves.

Pause on Focus works with both automatic descriptions and descriptions you request manually. It does not turn automatic descriptions on. If you previously turned automatic image descriptions off, they will remain off after the update, and you can still use Pause on Focus for manually requested descriptions.

The option controls only image descriptions spoken by the application. A separate screen reader controls its own speech, even when describing the same image, so moving focus may not stop all speech if both are active. Pause on Focus also has no effect on audio inside a video, which remains controlled by the video player. The option is available only on desktop; the mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

If a description continues after keyboard focus has visibly moved, please report it and include the action that moved focus. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that too—but you do not need to identify the source before reporting an issue. Knowing what action moved focus is more useful than receiving the contents of the image.

**New in this release: Pause on Focus**

This release adds a new option, Pause on Focus, to the Reading settings. It controls what happens to a spoken image description when you move keyboard focus to another control.

**What changes, and what stays the same**

Until now, a description that had started speaking kept going after focus moved on. That is still the default, so nothing changes unless you turn the new option on.

With Pause on Focus enabled, moving keyboard focus to a different control pauses the current description. Moving focus back to the image does not resume it. To hear the description again, use the existing Read Description command, which starts from the beginning.

The option is called "pause" because speech stops without discarding the saved description. It does not mean playback can pick up at the word where it stopped. The content of descriptions is not affected by this setting.

**What the option does not control**

Pause on Focus only applies to descriptions spoken by the application itself. Two other sources of speech are outside its reach:

- **A separate screen reader.** Speech from a screen reader is controlled by that reader, even when it is describing the same image. Turning on Pause on Focus will not necessarily silence all speech when focus moves.
- **Audio inside a video.** This remains controlled by the video player.

We compared two worksheets for subtracting background from fluorescence measurements. The current worksheet requires an operator to enter a blank reading separately for each sample; the proposed worksheet imports the blank reading from the instrument log to reduce transcription. The comparison assessed agreement between corrected values and the time required to produce them. It did not assess accuracy relative to a known true concentration, and no certified reference material was included.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session in a fixed order by solution number. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings; each aliquot was measured only once. The operator completed the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and could not see the imported results during manual entry. Although each solution contributed multiple aliquots, the worksheet comparison did not include independent repeat measurements of each aliquot’s instrument signal.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed at the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. All three differences occurred in the final solution, where a single blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log, making the manual corrected values 0.2 units lower. In a separate correction performed after the initial comparison, replacing the copied entry with the logged blank brought all 24 corrected values into agreement at the displayed precision.

The initial discrepancies are consistent with a transcription error propagated across three rows, rather than three independent transcription errors. They cannot be used to estimate a routine operator error rate: only one operator participated, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry. Agreement after correction supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement beyond the displayed precision, accuracy relative to true concentration, or correct blank assignment in future instrument logs.

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking—a seven-minute reduction in this session. These timings excluded instrument operation and the subsequent discrepancy investigation. The observed reduction applies to this session and its particular number of rows; whether it persists when log formats change or an operator must resolve a missing blank was not assessed.

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover might reduce the time water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before and four storms after a cover change. The three drains on the lower street received new covers; the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Allocation was not random: crews selected the lower street because it had received more complaints.

Fixed cameras recorded the minutes water remained above a painted reference line at each drain during each storm. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero indicates no visible water above the line, not an absence of runoff. Across the twelve observations for each street in each period, mean duration fell from 18 to 10 minutes on the lower street and from 9 to 7 minutes on the upper street. The lower street therefore showed an eight-minute reduction, compared with a two-minute reduction on the upper street. This larger reduction can inform further study, but the comparison does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Several factors limit interpretation. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. Neither street had a local gauge, and within-storm rainfall intensity was not measured. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Equally, cleaning cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets received it. These uncertainties, together with the nonrandom allocation of covers, leave the contribution of the cover change unresolved.

The camera records establish shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains during the later period. They do not establish increased drainage capacity, which was not directly measured, or fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot included no property-damage observations. Peak water depth could also change in a way that matters even if duration remained unchanged, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris quantities before cleaning. These measures would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and assessing the practicality of the camera-based duration measure. Staff reported that every recording could be scored; whether different scorers assign the same duration remains untested.

**Findings**

*What the pilot set out to test*

The pilot examined whether a different grate cover shortens the time water stands above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed across eight storms: four before a cover change and four after. The three drains on the lower street received new covers. The three drains on the upper street kept their existing covers. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so cover allocation was not random.

*What was measured*

A fixed camera at each drain recorded the number of minutes water remained above a painted reference line during each storm. A recorded duration of zero means no water was visible above the line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available for scoring.

Mean recorded duration, in minutes, across the twelve observations per street and period:

| Street | Before change | After change |
|---|---|---|
| Lower (covers changed) | 18 | 10 |
| Upper (covers retained) | 9 | 7 |

Durations fell at both sets of drains in the later period. The fall was larger on the street where covers were changed. That difference may help in deciding what to study next, but it does not by itself identify a cover effect.

*Why the comparison does not isolate a cover effect*

Two conditions changed alongside the covers, and neither can be separated from the cover change using the pilot's records.

- **Rainfall differed between periods.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier four. No gauge was installed on either street, and no within-storm intensity measurements exist. The pilot therefore cannot say how much of the shorter durations reflects lighter rain.
- **All six drains were cleaned on the day the covers were changed.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from every drain. Because the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, the cleaning does not automatically explain why the lower street improved more. For the same reason, it cannot be dismissed as irrelevant simply because both streets were cleaned. If the lower street had more debris to begin with, cleaning alone could account for part or all of the larger reduction there.

*What the measure does and does not capture*

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line. This is a narrower result than it may appear.

- It is not a measurement of drainage capacity, which was not directly measured.
- It is not a measurement of fewer flooded properties, which was not measured at all. The pilot collected no property-damage observations.
- It is not a measurement of peak water depth. A change in peak depth could matter even where recorded duration did not change, but peak depth was not extracted from the images.

*What remains unresolved*

The pilot does not establish whether the new cover shortens standing-water duration. The observed reduction on the lower street is consistent with a cover effect, with the effect of cleaning, with lighter rainfall, or with some combination. The design cannot distinguish among these.

One further uncertainty concerns the measure itself. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. The pilot has not tested whether different scorers assign the same duration to the same recording, so the reliability of the camera-based measure is unconfirmed.

*Proposed follow-up*

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains, install local rainfall gauges to record intensity on each street, and record the quantity of debris at each drain before any cleaning. Those steps would address the allocation, rainfall, and cleaning ambiguities described above. Rotation alone would not make storms identical, so rainfall measurement would still be needed to interpret differences between periods.

The existing recordings retain two uses. They describe standing-water duration at these six drains across these eight storms. They also provide material for testing whether independent scorers produce consistent durations, which would establish whether the camera-based measure is practical for future work.

## Findings

### Design and allocation

The pilot compared two streets over eight storms: four before and four after a change to a different grate cover. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their original covers and served as a comparison. The lower street was selected because crews had received more complaints there, so the cover change was not randomly assigned, and the two streets may differ in ways the pilot did not measure.

### Measurement

A fixed camera recorded, for each drain during each storm, the number of minutes that water stood above a painted reference line. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. A recorded duration of zero means no visible water above that line. It does not mean the drain received no runoff. The measure therefore reflects only water above the reference line, not total inflow or drainage performance.

Staff reported that all recordings could be scored. Scoring agreement between different scorers has not been tested, so the reliability of the duration measure is not yet established.

### Observed durations

On the lower street, the mean recorded duration across the twelve observations fell from 18 minutes before the cover change to 10 minutes after it. On the upper street, the mean fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The reduction was larger on the street where covers were changed.

This comparison does not isolate a cover effect. The lower street had higher durations before the change, and the two streets were not assigned comparably. The difference in reductions is a description of the recordings, not an estimate of the cover's effect.

### Factors that could explain the change

Several factors were present during the same period and cannot be separated from the cover change with the current data:

- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the earlier storms. No gauge was installed on either street, and within-storm intensity was not measured, so local rainfall differences between streets and periods are unknown.
- **Cleaning.** Crews cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because all six drains were cleaned, cleaning cannot account for the difference between the streets by itself. However, the initial quantity of leaves was not recorded, so cleaning may still have interacted with the cover change in ways the pilot cannot detect.

### What was not measured

- Drainage capacity was not measured directly.
- Flooding of properties was not measured. The pilot has no property-damage observations.
- Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even if recorded duration did not change, so the duration results do not establish whether depth changed.

The camera records show shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains in the later period. They do not establish the cause of that pattern, and they do not show any change in drainage capacity or flood outcomes.

### Unresolved questions

- Whether the cover change caused the reduction on the lower street, given non-random allocation and the differences in rainfall and cleaning.
- Whether the duration measure gives consistent results across different scorers.
- Whether changes in peak depth, drainage capacity, or flooding accompany the changes in duration.

### Proposed follow-up

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and leaf debris before cleaning. Rotation would address some of the present ambiguities, though it would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing these eight storms and for testing whether the camera-based duration measure can be applied in practice.

Returning keyboard focus to a cell puts the cursor back. Does it put the user back in context? This hypothetical study asked whether speaking the current row label after a note closes helps screen-reader users return to a table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each of two versions. One spoke the row label when the note closed. The existing version returned focus to the same cell without the added cue. Six participants used the cue version first; six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables, and table assignments were reversed for half of each order group.

We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval. We calculated each participant’s mean completion time for each version, then took the median of those twelve means. That median was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second gap is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test. These descriptive results do not establish a reliable speed benefit.

Did the cue help people feel oriented? Nine participants said it did in the closing interview. Four of those nine also described occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The same cue could help with orientation and interfere with listening. These reports describe participants’ experience; they are not a measured improvement in search performance.

The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but that does not tell us whether they wanted it enabled by default. We did not ask participants to choose a default.

The ordering scheme reduced the alignment between version and practice without removing every possible learning effect. A search strategy learned in the first task set may have carried into the second. The study also leaves two scope questions open: how less experienced users would respond, and how the cue would work in large tables. All participants were experienced, and the prototype tables fit within one screen.

For the product team, an orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. Added speech can also compete with ongoing speech. That competition needs attention even if a time difference eventually proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible, then test whether users can get the location information without losing speech they still need. We did not implement or test that behavior here. The present timings cannot serve as evidence for it.

Each version used different tables, and for half of each order group we reversed which tables went with which version. We timed from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was not timed.

## What we found

**Time.** The median of the twelve participant-level mean times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without. That is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Within individuals, seven participants had a lower mean with the cue, three a higher mean, and two were equal at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or run a significance test. So the direction is favorable, but we cannot say the difference is reliable.

**Interview feedback.** This is exploratory and is not measured performance. Nine participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also described times when the cue cut into speech they were still listening to. The other three reported no orientation benefit, though none asked for the cue to be removed. Does that mean they want it on by default? We can't say. Not asking for removal is not a preference for enabling it, and we never asked anyone to choose a default.

## What limits these results

- The ordering scheme reduced the alignment of version with practice, but it did not remove learning effects. Someone may have picked up a search strategy in the first set of tasks and carried it into the second.
- We recruited only experienced users. We don't know how less experienced users would respond.
- The prototype tables fit on one screen. We have no evidence about large tables.

## What it means for the design

An orientation benefit looks plausible for some users on these tasks. The same feedback shows that added speech can compete with speech already in progress. That is a design problem even if a time difference later proves reliable.

One option is to make the cue interruptible. We did not build or test that, so these timings are not evidence for it.

## Next step

The keypress-and-clock view told us how long the return took. It didn't tell us what the user was listening to when the cue arrived. The next test should follow that: use an interruptible cue, include large tables and less experienced users, add an explicit default-setting question, and plan the analysis (including an interval estimate on within-person differences) before collecting data.

# Diagrams Beside Questions or on a Reference Page: A Small Worksheet Comparison

*This report uses hypothetical evidence.*

## Summary

We compared two versions of a worksheet that asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B placed the same diagrams together on a reference page. In this comparison, a larger share of Version A answers earned full credit. The comparison cannot show that the layout caused the difference, because pupil assignment and teacher help were not controlled.

## What Was Compared

The two versions were identical in wording, diagrams, and question order. The only difference was where the diagrams appeared. Four classes used the materials during one lesson. Two classes received Version A and two received Version B. Teachers chose the version for their classes before they saw any pupil responses.

Teachers used the same written instructions and could answer pupil questions during the lesson. These exchanges were not recorded.

## Who Returned Worksheets

- **Version A:** 52 worksheets returned. Six pupils assigned this version were absent.
- **Version B:** 49 worksheets returned. Five pupils assigned this version were absent.

Only returned worksheets were analysed.

## How Answers Were Scored

A scorer who could not see the worksheet layout scored transcribed answers to the final explanation question. One point was awarded for stating that the amount of water was unchanged. One point was awarded for explaining that vessel shape changed the water level. A "fully credited" answer earned both points.

Ten transcribed answers were scored a second time by another scorer. The scorers agreed on nine. Discussion resolved the tenth before the final totals were compiled. This check helps describe the scoring procedure, but it is not a full reliability study.

## Results

| Score on the final question | Version A (52 worksheets) | Version B (49 worksheets) |
|---|---|---|
| Both points (fully credited) | 31 | 27 |
| One point | 15 | 16 |
| Zero points | 6 | 6 |

Fully credited answers made up a somewhat larger share of Version A worksheets than Version B worksheets. These scores come from one question. They do not measure pupils' general understanding of volume. No baseline task was scored, so the starting knowledge of the two groups is unknown.

## Limitations

- **Layout and class differences are mixed together.** Each version was used by two classes, so differences between classes could account for some or all of the result.
- **Teacher assistance was not recorded.** Teachers could answer questions during the lesson, and those exchanges are unknown.
- **Pupil assignment was not controlled.** Teachers chose the version for their classes, so the groups may differ in ways this comparison does not capture.
- **Absences and returns are excluded.** Eleven assigned pupils did not return worksheets, and the analysis does not include them.
- **Scoring reliability was checked only lightly.** Nine of ten double-scored answers matched, which is not enough for a full reliability estimate.
- **Preference was not measured.** No question asked which layout pupils preferred.

## What This Evaluation Shows and Does Not Show

This evaluation provides a concrete comparison of the returned answers. It shows that, in these classes, a somewhat larger share of answers earned full credit on the Version A layout. It does not show that the side-by-side layout was responsible for the difference.

A more controlled evaluation would need to record which version each pupil received, the classes and teachers involved, any teacher assistance during the lesson, absences and non-returns, and a baseline measure of starting knowledge. It would also need a fuller scoring reliability check and, if layout preference matters, a direct preference question.

| **Returned worksheets** | **52** | **49** |

*Percentages are of returned worksheets, rounded to the nearest whole number, so a column may not total exactly 100%.*

Version A had a somewhat larger share of answers awarded both points. The number of answers scoring zero was the same in each group.

These are scores on a single question. They are not a measure of pupils' general understanding of volume.

## What the results cannot tell us

- **Layout versus class differences.** Each version was used by different classes, and teachers chose which version each class received. Differences between the classes could account for some or all of the gap.
- **Starting knowledge.** No earlier baseline task was scored, so we do not know whether the two groups began with similar understanding.
- **Teacher assistance.** Teachers could answer questions during the lesson, and these exchanges were not recorded. The amount or kind of help may have differed between classes.
- **Scoring reliability.** The second-scorer check covered only ten answers.
- **Pupil preference.** Pupils were not asked which layout they preferred, so the evaluation says nothing about preference.

## Conclusion

In these four classes, the worksheet with a diagram beside each question was associated with a somewhat larger share of fully credited answers on the final question. The evaluation cannot separate the effect of layout from class differences or from classroom assistance.

What the completed work provides is a concrete comparison of these returned answers. It also gives a record of what a more controlled evaluation would need to capture:

- how classes come to receive each version
- pupils' starting knowledge
- teacher–pupil exchanges during the lesson
- a fuller check of scoring reliability

I recommend purchasing the two automatic warning signs for the underpass, on the condition that the same decision:

1. **Names a team responsible for monthly sensor checks.** Staff time for these checks has not yet been allocated, so this condition is not yet met.

## Rationale

**Signs warn; they do not keep water out.** The underpass sometimes fills with water before a maintenance crew can close the road. Signs can shorten that gap by alerting drivers sooner, but the drainage problem would remain.

The manual closure procedure covers this gap, and the monthly checks reduce how long a failure goes unnoticed.

**The permanent notice helps but does not solve the problem.** The proposal includes a notice telling drivers that water may be present even when the electronic sign is off. This informs drivers, but it does not stop drivers from overlooking or disregarding warnings.

**Warning equipment has value even though it is not complete protection.** Warning equipment cannot prevent every unsafe entry, but that is not a reason to reject it. The question is whether it reduces harm relative to the current situation, and the conditions above are what make that benefit reliable.

I propose revising the report template to make exclusions visible without changing which runs contribute to the reported mean. The summary would show the mean alongside the number of runs attempted and the number retained. A separate table, labeled “Record of exclusions,” would account for the difference by listing each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings would remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.

The current summary lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but it prevents readers from distinguishing a batch with no exclusions from one whose exclusions have simply disappeared from view. The proposed table would make those decisions inspectable. It would not require excluded readings to enter the mean or alter the existing exclusion rule.

Two examples illustrate why that distinction matters. A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result has not, for that reason alone, failed those conditions. Our existing rule therefore excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. The table would show how that rule was applied.

The table must also include excluded runs that produced no usable reading. Listing only excluded numeric values would conceal those failures and could make a difficult batch appear cleaner than it was. At the same time, stopped runs should not be treated as measured outcomes. Reporting attempted and retained counts beside the mean would preserve that distinction while allowing readers to account for every run.

Greater visibility carries a risk: readers may try to calculate a new mean from everything reported. Clearly labeling the table and recording every exclusion reason may reduce that risk, but cannot eliminate it. Including every raw reading would add detail unnecessary to inspecting the exclusion decisions and could make those decisions harder to follow. The proposed fields therefore provide an account of exclusions while leaving access to raw readings within the existing review process.

The proposal also adds reporting work, especially when one fault affects several runs. A shared explanation could cover such a group, provided each affected run still appears and is linked to that explanation. This would reduce repeated prose while keeping the batch’s history countable.

The tradeoff remains greater transparency at the cost of additional work and some risk of misinterpretation. Reviewers would still need to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing: a fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or resolve an ambiguous rule. It can make the decisions, including failures that yielded no reading, available for inspection.

# Revised Proposal: Reporting Excluded Runs in the Batch Summary

## Summary

I propose that the report template include a separate **exclusions table** that records every run removed from the reported mean, along with the reason for each exclusion. The summary would also state how many runs were attempted and how many were retained. This change makes the existing exclusion decisions visible. It does not change which runs are excluded, and it does not propose that every excluded reading enter the mean.

## Current Problem

The final summary lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. That presentation is convenient, but it leaves a reader unable to tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether exclusions were removed from view. A batch with three stopped runs and a batch with none can produce identical summaries.

## Two Kinds of Exclusion

The proposal depends on distinguishing two cases that the current rule already treats differently.

1. **Controller failure (run stopped).** The run was stopped because the temperature controller failed. The stated measurement conditions were not met, so the run is excluded.
2. **Completed run with an unusual result.** The run finished, but its result looks unusual. An unusual result alone does not show that the conditions failed. Under the existing rule, the run is **retained** unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion.

The exclusions table would expose how this rule was applied to each run. It would not change the rule.

## Proposed Table Contents

Each excluded run would appear as one row with four fields:

- **Run identifier**
- **Completion status** (for example, stopped or completed)
- **Reason** for exclusion, stated as documented
- **Usable reading exists** (yes or no)

Raw readings would not be added to this table. They would remain in the underlying record and stay available through the existing review process. Keeping the table to decisions makes the exclusions easier to scan.

## Runs With No Usable Reading

A table listing only excluded numeric values would omit runs that produced nothing usable. That omission could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. The summary therefore reports:

- the **number attempted**,
- the **number retained** beside the mean,

and the exclusions table accounts for the difference. Stopped runs are not counted as measured outcomes, which would distort the mean in the other direction.

## Shared Explanations for Grouped Faults

When one fault affects several runs, a shared explanation for that group may be used to reduce repeated prose. Each affected run must still appear as its own row, so the batch's history remains countable.

## Limits and Open Tradeoffs

This proposal does not solve every problem, and the following tradeoffs remain open:

- **Documented reasons may be weak or inaccurate.** A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording, and reviewers will still need to judge whether each stated reason is convincing.
- **The existing rule may be ambiguous.** The rule for retaining unusual completed results depends on a separately recorded fault. If that record is missing, the table cannot repair the ambiguity.
- **Readers may recalculate.** Showing failed runs may encourage readers to compute a new mean from everything visible. The table is labeled as a record of exclusions to discourage this, but the label may not prevent it.
- **Reporting takes time.** Recording each affected run adds work, especially when one fault affects many runs.

## Recommendation

Adopt the exclusions table as a proposal for discussion at the methods meeting. Decide whether the four-field format is sufficient, whether grouped explanations should be permitted, and how reviewers will judge documented reasons. The policy has not been adopted, and the existing exclusion rule remains unchanged.

That makes the mean easy to read, but a reader cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions simply disappeared from the summary. The proposal does not mean that excluded readings should enter the mean.

It also does not change the exclusion rule. Our existing rule excludes runs stopped by a temperature controller failure, because the stated measurement conditions were not met. It retains completed runs with unusual results, because an unusual result alone does not show that the conditions failed. Such a run is excluded only when a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies it. The table would show how this rule was applied.

**Why these columns and these counts**

A table of excluded numeric values would miss runs that produced no usable reading, which could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. That is why the table includes completion status and whether a usable reading exists. Listing every raw reading would be unnecessary for this purpose and could make the decisions harder to see. The opposite error is to count all stopped runs as measured outcomes, which distorts the results in a different way. Reporting attempted and retained counts beside the mean avoids both problems.

**What remains unresolved**

- **Recalculated means.** Showing failed runs may invite readers to calculate a new mean from everything in sight. Labeling the table as a record of exclusions responds to this, but the risk remains.
- **Judging the reasons.** Reviewers will still have to decide whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. It only makes the decisions available for inspection.
- **Reporting time.** The extra reporting takes time, especially when one fault affects several runs. One option is to permit a shared explanation for such a group while still listing each affected run. This would reduce repeated prose and keep the batch's history countable. Whether it saves enough time to justify the policy is not settled here.

# Proposal: Report excluded runs in a separate table

## Proposed policy

We propose that the report template add an **exclusions table** alongside the final summary. This is a proposal for discussion; it is not current practice.

1. **Exclusions table.** Every excluded run appears in a separate table, labeled as a record of exclusions. Each row gives:
   - run identifier
   - completion status
   - reason for exclusion
   - whether a usable reading exists
2. **Counts beside the mean.** The summary reports the number of runs attempted and the number retained next to the mean. The exclusions table accounts for the difference.
3. **Shared explanations for grouped faults.** When one fault affects several runs, a single shared explanation may cover the group. Each affected run still gets its own row.
4. **Raw readings stay out of the table.** They remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process.
5. **No change to the exclusion rule.** The table documents how the current rule was applied. It does not alter it.

## Problem

The final summary currently lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. A reader cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions simply disappeared from the summary.

## Why the existing rule is unchanged

The rule distinguishes two cases:

- **Stated conditions not met.** A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. It is excluded.
- **Unusual but completed.** An unusual result alone does not show that conditions failed. The run is retained unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion.

I am not proposing that every excluded reading enter the mean. The table makes visible how this rule was applied.

## Reasons for each design choice

- **Rows for runs, not just values.** A table of excluded numeric values would miss runs with no usable reading, which could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. The "usable reading exists" column covers these runs.
- **Attempted and retained counts.** Counting all stopped runs as measured outcomes would distort the results in the opposite direction. Reporting both counts keeps the denominator honest without treating stopped runs as measurements.
- **No raw readings in the table.** Including every raw reading is unnecessary for this purpose and could obscure the decisions the table is meant to show.
- **One row per run, even for shared faults.** This reduces repeated prose while keeping the batch's history countable.

## Tradeoffs and open questions

- **Recalculation risk.** Showing failed runs may invite readers to compute a new mean from everything listed. That may happen. The label and the full set of stated reasons are the mitigation; no reason should be omitted because it sounds repetitive. This does not eliminate the risk.
- **Reporting burden.** The additional reporting takes time, especially when one fault affects several runs. Shared explanations reduce the burden but do not remove it, because each run still needs a row. Whether this cost is acceptable is for the meeting to decide.
- **Limits of the table.** Reviewers must still judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. It makes the decisions available for inspection and nothing more.

## Decision requested

Should the template adopt the exclusions table, the attempted/retained counts, and the shared-explanation allowance as described, given the added reporting time and the recalculation risk?

**Proposal: report excluded runs in a separate table**

I propose that the report template show excluded runs in a separate table, with the reason for each exclusion. The final summary now lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. A reader therefore cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions were dropped from the summary. The proposal does not mean that every excluded reading should enter the mean.

**Why the table does not change the exclusion rule**

A run stopped because the temperature controller failed is different from a completed run with an unusual result. In the first case, the stated measurement conditions were not met. In the second, the unusual result alone does not show that they failed. Our existing rule excludes controller failures and keeps unusual completed results, unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies excluding them. The table would show how that rule was applied. It would not change the rule.

**What the table and summary would contain**

- The table would list, for each excluded run, its run identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. Raw readings would stay in the underlying record, available through the existing review process. Adding them to the table is unnecessary for this purpose and could make the decisions harder to see.
- The table would include runs with no usable reading. A table of excluded numeric values alone would miss those failures and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was.
- The summary would report the number of runs attempted and the number retained beside the mean, and the exclusions table would account for the difference. Counting all stopped runs as measured outcomes would distort the results in the opposite direction.
- Every reason would be listed, even if it repeats. When one fault affects several runs, I propose allowing a shared explanation for the group, with each affected run still appearing in the table. This reduces repeated prose and keeps the batch's history countable.

**Unresolved tradeoffs**

- Showing excluded runs may lead readers to calculate a new mean from everything in the report. It might. Labeling the table as a record of exclusions is the only safeguard I propose.
- Reviewers will still have to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. It makes the decisions available for inspection.
- The added reporting takes time, especially when the same fault affects several runs. The shared explanation reduces that cost but does not remove it.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then each \(d_n\ge0\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, first consider its partial sum:
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1}).
\]
Every intermediate term cancels, leaving
\[
S_N=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_{N+1}\) tends to zero, the partial sums \(S_N\) approach \(a_1\). By definition, this means that the series converges to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]
The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) has absolute value \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\) increases. Hence the infinite tail converges and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(a_n\to0\), there is an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) for every \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), we therefore have
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease is needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n=0\), and all the identities still hold. \(\square\)

**Theorem.** Let (a_n), n ≥ 1, be a sequence of real numbers that is nonnegative (a_n ≥ 0 for all n), nonincreasing (a_(n+1) ≤ a_n for all n), and has limit zero. Define d_n = a_n − a_(n+1). Then:

1. d_n ≥ 0 for every n.
2. The series d_1 + d_2 + d_3 + ... converges, and its sum is a_1.
3. For every integer N ≥ 1, the tail d_(N+1) + d_(N+2) + ... converges, and its sum is exactly a_(N+1).
4. For every ε > 0 there is an N such that the tail after N terms is less than ε.

**Before the proof: what "converges" means here.** A series converges when its partial sums approach a limit. The partial sum S_N is the sum of the first N terms. To say S_N → L means: for every ε > 0, there is an index beyond which every S_N lies within ε of L. We will verify this directly from the definition, using only the hypothesis a_n → 0. No convergence test or other theorem about series is needed.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: the terms are nonnegative.* Because the sequence is nonincreasing, a_(n+1) ≤ a_n, so d_n = a_n − a_(n+1) ≥ 0. (If two consecutive terms are equal, then d_n = 0. That is allowed. Nothing below requires d_n to be strictly positive.)

*Step 2: the partial sums telescope.* Fix N ≥ 1 and add up the first N terms:

```
S_N = d_1 + d_2 + ... + d_N
    = (a_1 − a_2) + (a_2 − a_3) + ... + (a_N − a_(N+1)).
```

Every term except the very first a_1 and the very last a_(N+1) appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. Those pairs cancel, leaving

```
S_N = a_1 − a_(N+1).        (A)
```

This is an exact identity for every N. It is the whole engine of the proof.

*Step 3: the series converges to a_1.* By (A), the distance from S_N to a_1 is

```
|S_N − a_1| = |−a_(N+1)| = a_(N+1),
```

using a_(N+1) ≥ 0. Now use the hypothesis a_n → 0 in its definition form: for a given ε > 0, there is an index K such that a_k < ε whenever k ≥ K. If N ≥ K, then N + 1 ≥ K as well, so

```
|S_N − a_1| = a_(N+1) < ε.
```

This is exactly the statement that S_N → a_1. So the series converges and its sum is a_1. This proves item 2.

*Step 4: the tail also telescopes.* Fix N ≥ 1. The tail after N terms is itself a series, d_(N+1) + d_(N+2) + ..., and its partial sums are the finite sums from n = N + 1 up to some M > N. Call that finite sum T_(N,M). It telescopes in the same way:

```
T_(N,M) = (a_(N+1) − a_(N+2)) + (a_(N+2) − a_(N+3)) + ... + (a_M − a_(M+1))
        = a_(N+1) − a_(M+1).        (B)
```

*Step 5: the tail converges to a_(N+1).* Keep N fixed and let M grow. By (B),

```
|T_(N,M) − a_(N+1)| = a_(M+1).
```

Given ε > 0, take the same K as in Step 3. If M ≥ K, then a_(M+1) < ε, so T_(N,M) is within ε of a_(N+1). Hence the tail partial sums converge to a_(N+1). That is, the tail after N terms has the exact value a_(N+1). This proves item 3.

*Step 6: the tail can be made small.* Given ε > 0, choose K as above and set N = max(1, K). Then N + 1 ≥ K, so the tail after N terms equals a_(N+1) < ε. This proves item 4.

**Remarks on edge cases.**

- If a_1 = 0, then every a_n satisfies 0 ≤ a_n ≤ a_1 = 0, so the sequence is identically zero. Every d_n is zero, identities (A) and (B) still hold, and the theorem says that the zero series sums to zero. No separate argument is needed.
- The proof never divided by anything, never assumed the a_n were strictly decreasing, and never assumed the d_n were positive. It used only three facts: a_n ≥ 0, a_(n+1) ≤ a_n, and a_n → 0.

**Why the result is useful.** The theorem turns a question about an infinite sum into a question about a single term of the original sequence. The partial sum S_N misses the true total by exactly a_(N+1). So if you want the sum accurate to within ε, you need only find an index where the original sequence has dropped below ε. ∎

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers with $a_n \ge 0$, $a_{n+1}\le a_n$ for every $n$, and $a_n \to 0$. Put $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms satisfies
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$
In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.** Since $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$, we have $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

*The partial sums telescope.* Fix an integer $N \ge 1$ and write out the sum of the first $N$ terms:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) \\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Every term after $a_1$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, except $a_{N+1}$, which appears only with a minus sign. So the partial sum is $a_1 - a_{N+1}$ exactly.

*The series converges to $a_1$.* To say that the series converges to $a_1$ means that the partial sums $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n$ come within any prescribed distance of $a_1$ once $N$ is large enough. By the identity above,
$$
|S_N - a_1| = |a_1 - a_{N+1} - a_1| = a_{N+1},
$$
where we dropped the absolute value because $a_{N+1} \ge 0$. Now use only what $a_n \to 0$ means: given $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ whenever $k \ge K$. For every $N \ge K$ we have $N+1 \ge K$, so
$$
|S_N - a_1| = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon .
$$
This is exactly the statement that $S_N \to a_1$, so $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = a_1$.

*The tail after $N$ terms.* Fix $N \ge 1$ and let $M > N$. The same cancellation gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) \\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$ is by definition the limit of these finite sums as $M \to \infty$. We show that the limit is $a_{N+1}$ directly. With $K$ chosen as before, for every $M \ge K$ we have $M+1 \ge K$, hence
$$
\Bigl|\,(a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}) - a_{N+1}\Bigr| = a_{M+1} < \varepsilon .
$$
Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, the finite sums converge to $a_{N+1}$, which proves
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$

*Making the tail small.* Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $K$ as above and take $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N \ge 1$ and $N + 1 \ge K$, so the tail equals $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$.

*Two remarks on the hypotheses.* If $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ forces every $a_n$ to be zero, every $d_n$ to be zero, and the identities above still hold with both sides equal to zero. If two consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding $d_n$ is zero. Nothing in the argument required a strict decrease, only $a_{n+1} \le a_n$. $\blacksquare$

# Telescoping Series and Tails

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Put
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \qquad (n \ge 1).$$
Then:

1. every $d_n$ is nonnegative;
2. the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$;
3. for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n$ converges and equals $a_{N+1}$;
4. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an integer $N \ge 1$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

---

## Proof

Throughout, recall what it means for a series to converge: a series $\sum_{n=p}^\infty c_n$ converges to $S$ when its partial sums $\sum_{n=p}^{M} c_n$ approach $S$ as $M \to \infty$. We will check this directly from the definition, using only limits of sequences.

**Step 1: Each $d_n$ is nonnegative.**
Since $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$. Subtracting gives $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

**Step 2: Write the partial sums as telescoping sums.**
Fix integers $M > N \ge 1$. We compute two finite sums. In each one, the terms cancel in pairs from the inside, so only the first and last endpoints survive.

For the first $N$ terms:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}) = a_1 - a_{N+1}. \tag{1}$$
Here $-a_2$ from the first bracket cancels $+a_2$ from the second, and so on, leaving $a_1$ and $-a_{N+1}$.

For the terms from $N+1$ to $M$:
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}$$
The same cancellation happens here, leaving $a_{N+1}$ and $-a_{M+1}$.

Identity (1) is the one with a fixed upper limit $N$. Identity (2) is the tail, with a fixed starting point $N+1$ and an upper limit $M$ that will grow.

**Step 3: The series converges to $a_1$.**
Let $S_N = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n$ be the partial sums of the series. By (1),
$$S_N = a_1 - a_{N+1}.$$
Since $a_n \to 0$, we have $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. Therefore $S_N \to a_1$. By definition, the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d_n$ converges and its sum is $a_1$.

**Step 4: The tail equals $a_{N+1}$.**
Fix $N \ge 1$. The partial sums of the tail are given by (2):
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.$$
As $M \to \infty$, we have $a_{M+1} \to 0$, because $M+1 \to \infty$ and $a_n \to 0$. The value $a_{N+1}$ does not depend on $M$, so the partial sums converge to $a_{N+1}$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1}.$$
This is the tail identity in the theorem.

**Step 5: The tail can be made small.**
Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $a_k \to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. Choose
$$N = \max(1, K).$$
Then $N + 1 > K$, so $N+1 \ge K$ and $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$. By Step 4, the tail is
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.$$
This proves the last claim. $\blacksquare$

## Remarks for students

- **Where each hypothesis is used.** The convergence in Steps 3 and 4 uses only $a_n \to 0$. The nonnegativity of $d_n$ comes from the nonincreasing property (Step 1). It is not needed for the algebra of the telescoping sums. Its role is to make the partial sums nondecreasing, which is a useful extra fact but not needed for the limit argument.

- **The case $a_1 = 0$.** Since $(a_n)$ is nonincreasing and nonnegative, $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n$ is zero. The identities (1) and (2) still hold, and the proof above applies without change. No special case is needed.

- **Equal consecutive terms.** If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The telescoping argument does not require the sequence to be strictly decreasing. Zero terms are allowed.

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Put $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}$. Then each $d_n \ge 0$, the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$. In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.**

*Nonnegativity.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$, so $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

*Partial sums.* Fix integers $M > N \ge 1$. We compute two finite sums by telescoping, meaning that consecutive terms cancel in pairs.

The first sum is

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1})
= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
$$

Each $a_k$ with $2 \le k \le N$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so only $a_1$ and $a_{N+1}$ remain.

The second sum is

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n
= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1})
= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
$$

The same cancellation occurs here, leaving only the first and last endpoints.

*Limits.* Since $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, the first identity gives

$$
\lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = \lim_{N\to\infty} (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_1.
$$

So the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$.

For a fixed $N$, the second identity gives, as $M \to \infty$,

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = \lim_{M\to\infty}\left(a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}\right) = a_{N+1} - 0 = a_{N+1}.
$$

This is the tail of the series after $N$ terms. It equals $a_{N+1}$.

*Small tails.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Because $a_k \to 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that $a_k < \varepsilon$ whenever $k \ge K$. Set $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N + 1 \ge K$, so the tail satisfies

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

*Remarks on degenerate cases.* If $a_1 = 0$, then nonnegativity and monotonicity force $a_n = 0$ for all $n$. Every $d_n$ is then zero, and the identities above still hold with both sides equal to zero. If two consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding $d_n$ is zero. The argument does not use strict decrease anywhere.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with limit \(0\). Define
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge 0\) for every \(n\), the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n\) converges to \(a_1\), and for every integer \(N\ge 1\),
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, the tail after \(N\) terms can be made smaller than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge 0\).

For any integers \(M>N\ge1\), the finite sums telescope:
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})
=a_1-a_{N+1},
\]
and
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]

Because \(a_n\to0\), the first identity shows that the partial sums \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n\) approach \(a_1\). Thus the series converges to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\). As \(M\) grows, \(a_{M+1}\to0\), so the second identity shows that the sums from \(N+1\) through \(M\) approach \(a_{N+1}\). This gives the tail formula
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the fact that \(a_n\to0\) lets us choose \(N\ge1\) so that \(a_{N+1}<\varepsilon\). The tail formula then gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n<\varepsilon.
\]
This also covers the case \(a_1=0\): nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n\) to be zero. Consecutive terms may be equal; in that case the corresponding \(d_n\) is simply zero.

In particular, for every \(\epsilon>0\), the tail is less than \(\epsilon\) for all sufficiently large \(N\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge 0\). For integers \(M>N\ge1\), cancellation of consecutive terms gives
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})
=a_1-a_{N+1},

and

=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]

As \(N\) tends to infinity, \(a_{N+1}\) tends to \(0\). Thus the first partial sum tends to \(a_1\), which proves that the series converges to \(a_1\). For fixed \(N\), let \(M\) tend to infinity in the second identity. Its right-hand side tends to \(a_{N+1}\), so the tail after \(N\) terms equals \(a_{N+1}\).

Now let \(\epsilon>0\). Since \(a_n\to0\), there is an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\epsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), the tail is \(a_{N+1}<\epsilon\).

If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity imply that every \(a_n=0\), and the identities still hold. Consecutive terms may also be equal; then the corresponding \(d_n=0\), so strict decrease is not needed.

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers that is nonnegative ($a_n \ge 0$), nonincreasing ($a_{n+1} \le a_n$), and satisfies $a_n \to 0$. Define
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \qquad (n \ge 1).$$
Then:

1. $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n$;
2. the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$;
3. for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_{N+1}$;
4. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

---

**Proof.**

*Step 1: The terms are nonnegative.* Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$. So $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$. Some $d_n$ may equal zero, namely whenever $a_{n+1} = a_n$. Nothing below needs strict decrease.

*Step 2: Partial sums telescope.* Recall that an infinite series converges to $S$ exactly when its sequence of partial sums converges to $S$. So we compute the partial sums. For any integer $N \ge 1$,
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}).
$$
Each intermediate term appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign: $-a_2$ cancels $+a_2$, $-a_3$ cancels $+a_3$, and so on up to $a_N$. Only the first and last terms survive:
$$
S_N := \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n = a_1 - a_{N+1}. \tag{1}
$$

*Step 3: The whole series converges to $a_1$.* By hypothesis, $a_{N+1} \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$. By (1), $S_N = a_1 - a_{N+1}$, and $a_1$ is a fixed number. Therefore $S_N \to a_1 - 0 = a_1$. This shows directly that the partial sums have a limit, and that the limit is $a_1$. So
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = a_1.
$$
We used only the definition of convergence of a series and the hypothesis $a_n \to 0$. No convergence test is needed.

*Step 4: Each tail converges to $a_{N+1}$.* Fix $N \ge 1$. The tail after $N$ terms is the series $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$. Its partial sums are the finite sums from $n = N+1$ to $n = M$, for $M > N$. These telescope in the same way:
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1}) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}
$$
Here $N$ is fixed and $M$ varies. As $M \to \infty$, $a_{M+1} \to 0$, so the right side of (2) tends to $a_{N+1}$. Hence the tail converges and
$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}. \tag{3}
$$
As a consistency check, (1) and (3) give
$$
\text{(first $N$ terms)} + \text{(tail)} = (a_1 - a_{N+1}) + a_{N+1} = a_1,$$
which agrees with Step 3.

*Step 5: The tail can be made smaller than any $\varepsilon$.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. The statement $a_k \to 0$ means, by definition, that there is an index $K$ such that $|a_k - 0| < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. Since $a_k \ge 0$, this says $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$.

Take $N = \max(1, K)$. The maximum with $1$ ensures that $N$ is a legitimate index $N \ge 1$. Then $N + 1 > K$, so $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$. By (3), the tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$, so it is less than $\varepsilon$.

Monotonicity also gives more. For any $N' \ge N$, the tail after $N'$ terms is $a_{N'+1} \le a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$. So once the tail is small, it stays small.

*Step 6: Edge cases.* If $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for all $n$, so every $a_n = 0$ and every $d_n = 0$. The identities (1)–(3) still hold, with every quantity equal to $0$, and the claims are trivially true. If some consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding $d_n$ are zero. The telescoping computations never divided by or relied on any $d_n$ being positive, so the proof is unaffected. $\blacksquare$

---

**Remark for students.** The key idea is that the series is built so that its partial sums have a closed form, equation (1). Once we have that formula, convergence of the series reduces to convergence of the sequence $(a_n)$ itself. That is why no outside convergence theorem was required.

**Claim.** Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence of real numbers with $a_n \to 0$. Put

$$
d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \qquad (n \ge 1).
$$

Then every $d_n$ is nonnegative, the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges to $a_1$, and for every integer $N \ge 1$ its tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$:

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$

In particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$, so $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$. If some consecutive terms are equal, the corresponding $d_n$ is zero. The argument below never uses a strict decrease, so this case needs no separate treatment.

*The series converges to $a_1$.* By definition, the series converges to $a_1$ when its partial sums

$$
S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
$$

tend to $a_1$ as $N \to \infty$. We compute $S_N$ by writing out the terms. Each $-a_{k}$ cancels the $+a_{k}$ that begins the next bracket, so only the first and last terms remain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_N
&= (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1})\\
&= a_1 - a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
|S_N - a_1| = |{-a_{N+1}}| = a_{N+1},
$$

where the last equality uses $a_{N+1} \ge 0$. Since $a_n \to 0$, the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $N \to \infty$. Hence $S_N \to a_1$, which means

$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = a_1.
$$

*The tail equals $a_{N+1}$.* Fix an integer $N \ge 1$. The tail $\displaystyle\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$ is itself a series, and its value is the limit, as $M \to \infty$, of its partial sums

$$
T_M = \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n \qquad (M > N).
$$

The same cancellation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_M
&= (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + (a_{N+2} - a_{N+3}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1})\\
&= a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $N$ is fixed, so $a_{N+1}$ is a fixed number, and only $a_{M+1}$ changes with $M$. Since $a_{M+1} \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$,

$$
|T_M - a_{N+1}| = a_{M+1} \to 0.
$$

Thus the tail converges and

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
$$

*The tail can be made smaller than $\varepsilon$.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Because $a_k \to 0$ and every $a_k \ge 0$, there is an integer $K$ such that

$$
a_k < \varepsilon \qquad \text{whenever } k \ge K.
$$

Take $N = \max(1, K)$. Then $N \ge 1$, so the tail identity applies, and $N + 1 > K$, so $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$. By the tail identity,

$$
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.
$$

Finally, if $a_1 = 0$, then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for every $n$, so all $a_n$ and all $d_n$ are zero. The identities above still hold, with every sum equal to $0$. $\blacksquare$

# Telescoping a Decreasing Sequence

**Theorem.** Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of real numbers that is nonnegative, nonincreasing ($a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for every $n$), and satisfies $a_n \to 0$. For each $n \ge 1$ put
$$d_n = a_n - a_{n+1}.$$
Then:

1. $d_n \ge 0$ for every $n$;
2. the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n$ converges, and its sum is $a_1$;
3. for every integer $N \ge 1$, the tail after $N$ terms, $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$, converges and equals $a_{N+1}$;
4. in particular, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ for which this tail is less than $\varepsilon$.

---

## What we have to prove

We need two definitions.

- **Limit of a sequence.** "$a_n \to 0$" means: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an index $K$ such that $|a_k| < \varepsilon$ whenever $k \ge K$. Our $a_k$ are nonnegative, so this says $0 \le a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$.
- **Sum of a series.** "$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = L$" means the partial sums
  $$S_N = \sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n$$
  satisfy $S_N \to L$ as $N \to \infty$. In other words, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $|S_N - L| < \varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large $N$.

So every statement about an infinite sum below is really a statement about a limit of finite sums. We will find those finite sums exactly and then take limits by hand.

**The idea.** When we add up the $d_n$, almost everything cancels:
$$S_N = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + (a_3 - a_4) + \cdots + (a_N - a_{N+1}).$$
Each of $a_2, a_3, \dots, a_N$ appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign. Only the first term $a_1$ and the last term $-a_{N+1}$ are left. A sum that collapses like this is called *telescoping*.

---

## Proof

### Step 1: Each $d_n$ is nonnegative.

The sequence is nonincreasing, so $a_{n+1} \le a_n$. Therefore $d_n = a_n - a_{n+1} \ge 0$.

### Step 2: A formula for the partial sums.

We claim that for every $N \ge 1$,
$$S_N = a_1 - a_{N+1}. \tag{1}$$

The cancellation pattern above shows why. To make it airtight, we use induction on $N$.

- *Base case $N = 1$:* $S_1 = d_1 = a_1 - a_2$, which is (1) with $N = 1$.
- *Inductive step:* suppose (1) holds for some $N$. Then
  $$S_{N+1} = S_N + d_{N+1} = (a_1 - a_{N+1}) + (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) = a_1 - a_{N+2},$$
  which is (1) with $N+1$ in place of $N$.

### Step 3: The series converges to $a_1$.

By (1), the distance from the partial sum to $a_1$ is
$$|S_N - a_1| = |-a_{N+1}| = a_{N+1}.$$
Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Because $a_n \to 0$, there is a $K$ with $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. If $N \ge K$, then $N + 1 \ge K$ as well, so
$$|S_N - a_1| = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.$$
This is exactly the definition of $S_N \to a_1$. Hence $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_n = a_1$.

### Step 4: The tail after $N$ terms equals $a_{N+1}$.

Fix an integer $N \ge 1$. The tail $\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n$ is itself a series. Its partial sums are, for $M > N$,
$$T_M = \sum_{n=N+1}^{M} d_n.$$
These are the terms of $S_M$ that are not already in $S_N$, so (1) gives
$$T_M = S_M - S_N = (a_1 - a_{M+1}) - (a_1 - a_{N+1}) = a_{N+1} - a_{M+1}. \tag{2}$$
You can also see (2) directly: $T_M = (a_{N+1} - a_{N+2}) + \cdots + (a_M - a_{M+1})$ telescopes in the same way.

Now keep $N$ fixed and let $M \to \infty$. From (2),
$$|T_M - a_{N+1}| = a_{M+1}.$$
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and choose $K$ as in Step 3. For every $M$ with $M > N$ and $M \ge K$, we have $M + 1 \ge K$, so $|T_M - a_{N+1}| = a_{M+1} < \varepsilon$. Therefore $T_M \to a_{N+1}$, which means
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.$$

### Step 5: The tail can be made smaller than any $\varepsilon > 0$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $K$ with $a_k < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$, and set $N = \max(1, K)$. The maximum only guarantees that $N \ge 1$, so the theorem's notion of "tail after $N$ terms" applies. Since $N + 1 > N \ge K$, we get $a_{N+1} < \varepsilon$. By Step 4,
$$\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1} < \varepsilon.$$
The same reasoning works for every $N \ge \max(1, K)$, not just this one. $\blacksquare$

---

## Remarks

- **No outside convergence test was needed.** We never had to argue abstractly that the series converges. Telescoping gave the exact value of every partial sum, (1) and (2). After that, convergence reduced to the hypothesis $a_n \to 0$ and the definition of a limit.
- **Where each hypothesis was used.** "Nonincreasing" was used only in Step 1, to get $d_n \ge 0$. "$a_n \to 0$" was used in Steps 3–5. "Nonnegative" let us write $|a_k| = a_k$, so we could drop absolute values.
- **The case $a_1 = 0$.** Then $0 \le a_n \le a_1 = 0$ for every $n$, so every $a_n$ and every $d_n$ is $0$. The formulas still hold: the series sums to $0 = a_1$, and each tail is $0 = a_{N+1}$. Nothing in the proof needs to change.
- **Equal consecutive terms.** If $a_n = a_{n+1}$ for some $n$, then $d_n = 0$. The proof never needed $d_n > 0$, so strict decrease is not required anywhere.

\[

\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N} d_n
&= (a_1-a_2)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\

\[

&= (a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&= a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

\]

The second identity shows that, with $N$ fixed, $T_M$ differs from $a_{N+1}$ by exactly $a_{M+1}$. If $M>N$ and $M\ge K$, then $M+1>K$, and $(*)$ gives

\[
0\le a_{N+1}-T_M = a_{M+1}<\varepsilon .
\]

Hence $T_M\to a_{N+1}$ as $M\to\infty$. The tail series therefore converges, and

\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}.
\]

\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} d_n = a_{N+1}<\varepsilon . \qquad\blacksquare
\]

=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]

Because \(a_n\to0\), this difference tends to zero. In other words, the partial sums approach \(a_1\). This is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n

=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.

The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\). Hence the infinite tail exists and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to0\) provides an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), therefore,
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
